cards.body: Traditional software follows rules a human wrote: if X, then Y. Machine learning flips it — you feed the computer examples, and it writes its own rules. Spam filters don't list every spam phrase; they learn what spam looks like from millions of emails.
cards.title: Rules vs. learning from examples

cards.body: Every ML problem has two ingredients. Features are the inputs the model sees (an email's words, a house's size). Labels are the answers it must learn to predict (spam or not, the price). Get the labels wrong and the model learns the wrong lesson — garbage in, genius out is not a thing.
cards.title: Features are the clues, labels are the answers

cards.body:
You always split your data:
• Training set — the examples the model learns from.
• Test set — examples it has never seen, used only to grade it.
A student who memorizes the practice exam but blanks on the real one learned nothing. The test set is the real exam.

When someone says 'AI', ask: what's the label? Translation, recommendations, face unlock — every ML system is just predicting some label from some features. Find those two and the magic disappears (in a good way).

choices: It learns patterns from data instead
cards.explain: ML's whole trick is learning rules from examples rather than having a human hand-write every rule.

cards.body: A neuron is embarrassingly simple: it multiplies each input by a weight, adds them up, and passes the result through a squish function. Intelligence doesn't live in one neuron — it emerges from millions of them voting together through layers.
cards.title: One neuron is dumb; a million aren't

cards.body: Layers are an assembly line. Early layers detect simple stuff (edges in an image), middle layers combine them (shapes, textures), late layers decide (that's a cat). Deep learning just means many layers — depth, not mystery.
cards.title: Layers: an assembly line for patterns

cards.body:
Training in one breath:
1. The net guesses, and gets it wrong.
2. Math measures the error.
3. Gradient descent nudges every weight a tiny step downhill toward less error.
4. Repeat millions of times.
That's it. All of modern AI is glorified downhill walking.

Overfitting is when the model memorizes the training data instead of learning the pattern — like a student who memorized last year's exam word for word. It aces training and face-plants on anything new. More diverse data is the cure.

cards.explain: 'Deep' refers to depth — many stacked layers, each building on the last. More layers, more abstract patterns.

cards.body: An LLM does exactly one thing: predict the next token. A token is a chunk of a word ('un' + 'believ' + 'able'). Feed it 'the cat sat on the', and it bets 'mat' is likeliest next. Everything — essays, code, jokes — is next-token prediction at massive scale.
cards.title: LLMs do one trick: guess the next chunk

cards.body: Prompts matter because the model has no goals of its own — it just continues your text. 'Explain like I'm five' vs 'give a formal proof' produce wildly different outputs from the same model. The prompt is the steering wheel; the model is the engine.
cards.title: The prompt is the steering wheel

cards.body: Hallucination isn't a bug in the usual sense — it's the model doing its job. It optimizes for plausible-sounding text, not truth. Ask for a paper that doesn't exist and it will invent a convincing citation, because 'convincing' is what it was trained to produce.

Never trust an LLM's facts without checking — use it for drafting, brainstorming, and explaining, then verify claims yourself. Treat it like a brilliant intern with total confidence and zero accountability.

cards.explain: One trick, scaled up: guess the most likely next chunk of text, over and over. No search, no rulebook.
cards.q: What is the single thing an LLM is trained to do?
